Same scam. 2 countries. Why Canadians don’t get their money back
Bank scammer confronted by CBC Marketplace
Two people described the same financial scam to the police and their banks over the past year. The only difference was where they lived — one in Canada, the other in the U.K.
And that determined what happened next.
Asif Mohammed lost $7,200 this spring and never got it back. Meanwhile, Samantha Bradshaw was out £11,000 (nearly $21,000 Cdn) but her financial institution reimbursed the money within days.

That's because British banks are required by law to make most of their customers whole when money is lost to a scam — often returning the sum within days of making a claim. In contrast, Canadian banks have no such legal obligation, leaving scam victims here largely unprotected.
As CBC’s Marketplace found out, it also means British banks are incentivized to crack down on fraudsters in a way Canadian banks are not.
Read our full investigation from David Common and Nelisha Vellani.
Toronto Crime Stoppers pauses program after CBC investigation reveals details of data leak
Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database
Toronto Crime Stoppers is pausing its program effective immediately, said its chair, Sean Sportun, in a statement sent late Wednesday evening.

The news follows an exclusive CBC investigation from earlier that day revealing information from more than 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years was exposed in a massive data breach. It was the first time precise figures were made public showing the severity of the information exposed, as well as how many Canadian tipsters have been compromised.

Up until the investigation was published, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) and individual chapters had not spoken out about the extent of the breach, only saying they awaited a detailed report from Navigate360, the U.S.-based third-party company that manages its data through platform P3.

Toronto Crime Stoppers now says it has removed the "Tip Submit" feature from its website and will no longer accept or process any new information intended for the program. It has also advised Navigate360 to immediately suspend the intake function for the Toronto Crime Stoppers chapter from its platform.
In the statement, the organization advised the public not to send tips by phone, online or through its app "until we have a safer way to protect you."

"People in Toronto have come to Toronto Crime Stoppers because we promised they could stay anonymous. This week’s reporting shows that for some of them, that promise was broken. We are deeply sorry," Sportun said in a statement.
The Toronto Police Service also announced in a statement Wednesday evening that it has "temporarily suspended its use of Crime Stoppers" until further review.
MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada amid mounting harms
Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There’s a push to change that
For T.S., a 22-year-old Ontario man recovering from a gambling problem, widespread advertising for online casinos and betting during sports broadcasts is "frustrating."
"Imagine you're an alcoholic and there was a beer ad during every show you watched," he told CBC News.
His gambling started three years ago as a fun Friday night activity with friends, but it escalated.
One night last year he found himself locked inside a bathroom, losing it all — having bet away $14,000.
T.S., who CBC has agreed not to name, says he quickly sought treatment and hasn't gambled since. But during his spree, all those ads fuelled him to gamble more.
"It certainly … would trigger me to go back and place another bet."
Politicians in Ottawa are moving to curb the widespread advertising currently seen across sports broadcasts, social media and online video games.

The federal standing committee on Canadian heritage meets next week to vote on Bill S-211, a law that proposes to rein in the ads across the country, amid new findings of increased addiction and gambling-related suicides in Ontario.
A new analysis for CBC News shows Canadians continue to be bombarded with betting promotions during sports broadcasts.

The new analysis also confirms little has changed since a CBC Marketplace study in 2024 revealed viewers were bombarded with thousands of ads and product placements in five NHL games (up to three per minute).

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bobby Hristova is an award-winning investigative reporter with CBC's Marketplace. He writes The Watchdog, Marketplace's weekly newsletter. He's passionate about investigative work and accountability journalism that drives change — and he believes your story can help others. He worked with CBC Hamilton from 2019 to 2024 and also worked with CBC Toronto's Enterprise Team.
